cards.title: Measure purchase conversion rate, not raw key event rate
cards.summary: GA4's 'key events' bundle purchases with other actions, so you must manually filter to the purchase event before reading any conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Judging whether your store's or a channel's conversion rate is healthy before making merchandising or media-spend decisions.
steps: Understand the trap: in GA4, key events are not only purchase events; page views, add-to-carts and other actions can be marked as key events.
When you add the 'session key event rate' metric to any report, drill into the metric and set the event filter explicitly to 'purchase'.
Only then read the percentage as your conversion rate.
Sanity-check the result against total revenue in the same table so you are not reading a rate built on the wrong event set.
Re-check this filter after any GA4 configuration change, since the key-event set can drift over time.
caveats: The source's own store showed ~1.7% conversion rate after filtering to purchase; treat that as an example, not a benchmark.
GA4's interface changes over time, so verify the current click path before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Find conversion rate by traffic channel
cards.summary: Customize the Traffic Acquisition report to add session key event rate filtered to purchase so you can compare conversion performance across organic, CPC and email.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to shift acquisition budget or fix a channel that drives traffic but no sales.
steps: Go to Reports -> Life Cycle -> Traffic Acquisition.
Click 'Customize report', then under Metrics add 'Session key event rate'.
Filter that metric to the purchase event only, as raw key events overstate conversion.
Optionally add the 'medium' dimension to split further, e.g. distinguishing organic from CPC and identifying specific senders like an email platform.
Save the customized report so you can return to it without redoing the setup.
Compare conversion rate across channels: a channel with strong sessions but weak purchase rate is a targeting or landing-page problem, not a volume problem.
caveats: Channel grouping depends on correct UTM tagging; untagged campaigns will fall into the wrong bucket and distort the comparison.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Read engaged sessions as a traffic-relevance signal
cards.summary: GA4 counts a session as engaged when it lasts longer than 10 seconds, making it a quick relevance check on the traffic you are buying or earning.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether paid or organic traffic is actually reaching a page that matches the visitor's intent.
steps: Open the Traffic Acquisition report and read engaged sessions, engagement rate and average engagement time by channel.
Treat a very low engaged-session count on a channel as a signal that visitors are not finding what they searched for or that the landing page does not match the query.
Cross-reference with the Landing Pages report to see whether specific entry pages are dragging the channel's engagement down.
If paid traffic shows low engagement, check ad-to-landing-page message match before increasing spend.
If organic shows low engagement, review whether the ranking page's content and product selection match the search intent.
caveats: The 10-second threshold is GA4's definition of an engaged session, not a performance target you must hit.
Low engagement can also come from bot traffic or mis-tagged campaigns, so rule those out first.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Compare product-page conversion rates in the Landing Pages report
cards.summary: Add the purchase-filtered session key event rate to the Landing Pages report to see which product pages convert and which are leaking.
cards.use_when: Deciding which product pages need new copy, photography or price tests, or whether a page's traffic is simply mismatched.
steps: Go to Reports -> Engagement -> Landing Pages.
Click to edit the report and add the 'session key event rate' metric.
Filter the metric to the purchase event so the rate reflects buyers, not all key events.
Compare rates across your top product pages, looking for outliers far above or far below the others.
Interpret a low outlier as one of three causes: wrong traffic being sent to that page, a page that needs more work, or a product that is simply less appealing.
Investigate the cause before rewriting the page, since a traffic mismatch will not be fixed by design changes.
caveats: Small traffic volumes produce noisy rates; a page with a handful of sessions can look dramatically better or worse than it is.
Shopify's native analytics does not expose this page-level conversion rate, which is why the GA4 setup matters.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Diagnose funnel drop-off with the Purchase Journey report
cards.summary: The Monetization -> Purchase Journey report shows drop-off between session start, product view, add to cart, checkout and purchase so you can localise friction.
cards.use_when: Investigating where shoppers abandon so you can decide whether to fix navigation, cart, pricing or checkout trust.
steps: Go to Reports -> Monetization -> Purchase Journey and set your date range.
Read the step-by-step progression: session started, viewed product, added to cart, began checkout, purchased.
Treat the drop between session started and viewed product as largely normal—many visitors are just browsing.
Focus on the drops between add to cart, checkout and purchase, which are the diagnostically meaningful ones.
If many sessions never view a product, question collection clarity, navigation and search rather than the product pages themselves.
If shoppers drop between add to cart and checkout, suspect the cart page; if they drop between checkout and purchase, suspect shipping cost, trust or checkout process friction.
caveats: In the source example, roughly half of sessions viewed a product, most viewers added to cart, 63% of those began checkout and 50% of those purchased—these are illustrative, not targets.
Funnel steps depend on correct event tracking; missing add-to-cart or checkout events will show fake drop-offs.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Segment traffic by channel and medium together
cards.summary: Adding the medium dimension to the Traffic Acquisition report gives a second layer of detail, separating CPC from paid social and identifying specific senders like your email platform.
cards.use_when: Working out which specific paid or owned channel is producing sessions, before shifting budget or cadence.
steps: Open Traffic Acquisition and customize the report to display the medium dimension alongside session primary channel group.
Read the resulting rows to separate, for example, CPC campaigns from paid social placements and email sends.
Use the split to spot channels that consume budget or send volume without contributing purchases.
Combine with the purchase-filtered session key event rate to rank mediums by conversion, not just volume.
Save the view and re-check on a regular cadence rather than a single snapshot.
caveats: Medium values come from UTM parameters, so discipline in tagging determines whether this view is trustworthy.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Customize and save GA4 reports instead of reading defaults
cards.summary: Default GA4 tables omit the metrics you actually need; adding metrics under Customize Report -> Metrics and saving the view is the core workflow.
cards.use_when: Setting up a repeatable weekly reporting routine you do not want to rebuild each time.
steps: Open the report you want to change (Traffic Acquisition or Landing Pages are the reported starting points).
Click 'Customize report', then under Metrics add the fields you care about—session key event rate, engagement rate, average engagement time, total revenue.
Apply the metric, then set any event filters (notably purchase) so the numbers mean what you think they mean.
Save the customized report so it persists for future sessions.
Use the Library section to add or remove report elements if the default navigation is distracting, but keeping defaults is also a valid choice.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that key events include more than purchases, so any added key-event-based metric must be filtered before interpretation.
GA4's customization interface is subject to change; confirm current labels before writing internal documentation.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Use GA4 to fill gaps Shopify analytics leaves
cards.summary: GA4's traffic-source and per-page detail exceeds what the Shopify dashboard reports, so treat GA4 as the channel and page diagnostic layer and Shopify as the order-level view.
cards.use_when: Deciding which analytics tool to check for a given question about traffic or page performance.
steps: Keep the GA4 home dashboard for a quick overview only; the source notes most of those numbers duplicate Shopify.
Use GA4 Reports for channel-level traffic detail, engagement quality and per-landing-page conversion, which Shopify does not provide at this granularity.
Use Shopify for order and product sales totals, and GA4's e-commerce purchases report to explore product-level purchase behaviour.
If you run Google Ads, link GA4 to Google Ads and to your store through the Shopify integration so advertising results surface inside GA4.
Walk the Life Cycle report set in GA4 as a standing review habit rather than relying on the default home screen.
caveats: Numbers will differ between GA4 and Shopify due to different attribution and session definitions; decide which system is your source of truth per question.
cards.source_name: Google Analytics 4 For eCommerce 2025 ( Perfect for beginners).docx

cards.title: Read GA4's AI Insights for quick answers, not deep analysis
cards.summary: The Insights tool offers predefined suggested questions and short answers, useful for fast orientation when you are new to the platform.
cards.use_when: Getting a fast orientation answer such as which countries your visitors come from, before digging into a full report.
steps: Open the Insights tool from the GA4 home area and browse the suggested questions.
Pick a question relevant to the decision at hand—for example demographics or country distribution.
Read the short answer as a starting pointer, then verify in the underlying report before acting on it.
Do not treat the predefined question list as comprehensive; it is limited by what GA4 offers.
caveats: The question set is limited and predefined by GA4; it cannot answer arbitrary business questions.
The source treats this as a convenience only, not a substitute for the Traffic Acquisition and Landing Pages reports.
